opus-5.5.text:
I think of research and engineering as two different modes of working toward the same goal, and they need different mindsets.

Research is about reducing uncertainty. When you start a research project, you don't know whether the idea will work. Most of the time it doesn't. So the job is to explore, to form hypotheses, run quick experiments, and find out as fast as possible whether there's something real there. A good researcher is comfortable with failure and with ambiguity, and is willing to throw away a lot of work once they learn the direction is wrong. What you produce is mostly knowledge: this approach works, that one doesn't, and here's why.

Engineering starts once you have enough confidence that something can work. Then the question changes from "is this possible?" to "how do we make it reliable, scalable, and useful for many people?" That takes a different kind of discipline. You care about robustness, edge cases, efficiency, maintainability, and making sure the system works not only on your demo but on millions of real inputs. The success criteria are much more concrete.

In practice, especially in AI today, the boundary has gotten blurry. Many of the big advances, like scaling up generative models or building world models, are research questions that you can't answer without serious engineering. You can't test whether a model trained on huge amounts of video learns physical understanding unless you can build the data pipelines and the training infrastructure to do it. So engineering has become a tool for doing research. And the reverse is true too: when you deploy a system, you find failure modes that turn into new research problems.

So I don't see one as more important than the other. The best teams I've worked with have people who can switch between the two modes, or at least respect each other deeply. Researchers need to understand what it takes to make something real, and engineers need to understand why exploration sometimes looks inefficient. When those two work closely together, progress happens much faster.

r001.rationale: The response describes research as reducing uncertainty through hypotheses and experiments, but does not identify asking the right question as research’s most important part.

r002.rationale: It says engineering can support research by enabling large-scale tests, but does not characterize implementation as demonstrating that the research question itself is the right one.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of them as two halves of the same thing, and at NVIDIA we've really tried not to draw a hard line between them.

Research is about asking the right question. You're trying to figure out what is possible, what the limits are, which direction is worth betting on. A lot of that is exploration, and most of what you try doesn't work. That's fine. The output of research is understanding. Sometimes it's a paper, sometimes it's just the knowledge that a certain path is a dead end so the team doesn't spend six months on it.

Engineering is about making the thing actually work, at scale, reliably, for real people. A result in a paper on a small benchmark is one thing. A model that trains stably on tens of thousands of GPUs, serves customers, and doesn't fall over when the data distribution shifts is a completely different thing. Engineering is where you discover that the beautiful idea has a hundred ugly details, and you have to solve every one of them.

What I've learned, especially building large generative models, is that in this era you can't separate them. The scale is the research. If your infrastructure can't handle the experiment, you can't ask the question. The person who writes the data pipeline is shaping the science as much as the person who designs the loss function. So when I hire, I look for researchers who respect engineering, and engineers who are curious about why something works, not just that it works. The best people I've worked with move back and forth. They'll write a paper one quarter and spend the next quarter fixing throughput, and they see both as the real work.

If I had to put it in one sentence: research tells you where to go, engineering gets you there, and today neither one can move very far without the other.

r001.rationale: The response says research is about asking the right question and describes it as its central purpose.

r002.rationale: It describes engineering as making ideas work at scale, but does not say implementation demonstrates that a research question was the right one.

astra-6.text:
I think research and engineering are closely connected, but they have different goals. Research is about reducing uncertainty: can we solve this problem, and what new idea would make that possible? Engineering is about turning an idea into something reliable and useful.

In research, a failed experiment can still be valuable if it teaches you something. In engineering, showing that something works once is only the beginning. You need to make it work consistently, within constraints like compute, latency, and cost.

The boundary is not sharp, though. Building a system often exposes problems that lead to new research, and good engineering lets you test research ideas more effectively. I see them as a cycle: research opens up possibilities, and engineering helps us understand which possibilities actually deliver value.

r001.rationale: The response describes research as reducing uncertainty and finding ideas, but does not identify asking the right question as research’s most important part.

r002.rationale: It says engineering turns ideas into reliable systems and helps test research ideas, but does not say implementation demonstrates that the research question itself is the right one.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research and engineering are closely connected, but they have different goals. Research is about exploring uncertainty: Can we do something that we couldn’t do before? Can we find a better approach? In that process, failure is useful because it helps us understand the problem.

Engineering is about turning an idea into something reliable and useful. A method might work in a research experiment, but making it work consistently under real constraints—compute, latency, cost—requires a different kind of creativity.

The two should inform each other. Research opens up possibilities, and engineering reveals which assumptions hold in practice. When that feedback loop works well, practical challenges lead to new research questions, and research advances become things people can actually use.
